meta.purpose: Every statement in Style Guide v1.4 that is a rule or a value, extracted verbatim and machine-readable. This is the approved steer, committed. Joined to The Decision Book for tier and reasoning.
meta.quoting: The `statement` field is verbatim from v1.4. Table rows are reassembled as 'row label · <Column>: <cell>' using the guide's own column headers. Every row was string-matched back to the source: zero unverified.
meta.blocked: 15 statements cannot be encoded as written because v1.4 contradicts itself. See contradictions[] — 3 resolved on accessibility grounds, 7 awaiting Carly, 5 bookkeeping.

contradictions.a: Teal is never a logo colour on a light ground — 1.52:1 on white. Pink (7.42:1) and violet (7.64:1) are the accents that clear it.
contradictions.finding: 7.42 and 7.64 are the ink-ground ratios, read from the wrong column. On white, pink and violet both fail 3:1.
contradictions.resolution: On a light ground the wordmark is blue (8.59:1) or ink. The repo's asset set already reflects this.

contradictions.a: Every accent is a black-text surface. Every ground is a white-text surface. There are no exceptions and no judgement calls.
contradictions.b: Chalk #F3F3F3 · INK OR CHARCOAL TEXT · 17.52:1 — White #FFFFFF · INK OR CHARCOAL TEXT · 19.44:1
contradictions.finding: White on chalk is 1.11:1. The headline rule is false for 2 of the 5 grounds.
contradictions.resolution: The rule holds for the dark grounds — blue and ink. Chalk and white are reading grounds taking ink or charcoal. Also wrong in the nightlife-culture-design skill, non-negotiable 1.

contradictions.a: Never below 16pt on screen or 14pt in print.
contradictions.finding: A slide label is on screen, all caps, and 14pt.
contradictions.resolution: 16pt on screen. 14pt is the print floor applied to the wrong medium.

contradictions.a: Never brand accents · Pink, teal, violet, butter and coral are surfaces. Only the ramp encodes data.
contradictions.finding: #FFDE6B is byte-identical to the butter accent.

contradictions.a: More than about 55% covered means it is two slides.
Full-bleed band · Accent or ink, edge to edge · Slides and covers.

contradictions.finding: 1.5% of a 1280px slide is 19px — 3-5x below the stated minimum.

contradictions.a: Cover and back page only. Never in a running header.
contradictions.b: The guide places the wordmark in its own masthead and footer.
Ten are named; the contrast matrix carries nine.

contradictions.resolution: 2.44 is pure #000000, not a token. Use ink, 2.26:1.

contradictions.a: Line height resolved to a single 1.5-1.6 floor (v1.1)
contradictions.b: Line height scoped by style class (v1.2)
contradictions.resolution: Mark v1.1 superseded. Scoped values are current.

contradictions.a: WCAG SC 1.4.8 sets 1.5 as the floor
contradictions.b: Meet WCAG 2.2 AA as the minimum standard
contradictions.resolution: 1.4.8 is AAA. Cite 1.4.12 or drop the citation and keep the value.

contradictions.a: State publication date, data period, geography and population.
contradictions.b: Code, reference period, geography and boundary vintage.
contradictions.resolution: Take the superset of all six fields.
Keep the ban. Drop the slide column — it specifies an object that cannot exist.

statements.statement: This guide has three layers. Use the first to understand what Nightlife Culture stands for, the second to express it consistently, and the third to produce accessible, evidence-led outputs.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Brand foundation · Purpose: Defines our territory, beliefs, offer, audiences and method. · How stable is it?: Relatively stable. Review when the business proposition changes.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Expression system · Purpose: Defines voice, tone, language, visual identity and imagery. · How stable is it?: Evolves through use, feedback and commissions.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Production system · Purpose: Defines accessibility, evidence, documents, decks, spreadsheets, charts and AI controls. · How stable is it?: Operational and testable. Update when standards or tools change.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Accessibility does not dilute the brand. It decides where the brand should live.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Nightlife Culture is a creative policy, research and design studio working across nightlife, music, culture, place and the systems that shape them.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: We combine cultural literacy, lived experience, policy knowledge, evidence and human-centred design to help places and cultural ecosystems understand value, align people, make stronger decisions and build practical routes forward.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: A creative policy studio for nightlife, music, culture and cities.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: We help places and cultural ecosystems understand what creates value, what conventional systems miss, and what conditions people need to thrive. We turn lived experience, sector knowledge, data and creative practice into evidence, shared asks, practical frameworks and delivery routes.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Nightlife is culture. It is made by artists, promoters, DJs, producers, crews, venue and festival teams, bar and door teams, technicians, audiences, organisers, freelancers, communities and informal networks.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Nightlife spaces are not passive backdrops. They are talent incubators, knowledge banks, gathering places, workplaces, testing grounds, civic assets and cultural value generators.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Nightlife Culture is not defined by a conventional category alone. It can perform functions associated with consultancy, research, advocacy, convening, service design and policy development. The distinctive proposition is the combination: a studio practice that gathers people, builds evidence, makes value visible and designs practical routes forward.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Nightlife, music and culture · Typical questions: What creates value, identity, belonging, opportunity and collective joy?
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Economic development and place · Typical questions: How do culture and the night contribute to local growth, high streets, employment and investment?
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Policy, planning and governance · Typical questions: Where are rules, institutions, incentives and responsibilities misaligned with lived reality?
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Public health, safety and access · Typical questions: What conditions help people participate, work and travel safely and with dignity?
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Evidence, evaluation and data · Typical questions: What is counted, what is missing, and what can be known responsibly?
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Human-centred and systems design · Typical questions: How can people shape decisions, tools and infrastructure that affect them?
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: clearer evidence
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: stronger shared language
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: better decisions
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: usable tools and frameworks
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: more capable relationships and networks
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: transparent assumptions and methods
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: a practical route to implementation
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: The method is flexible enough for research, strategy, policy, feasibility, economic development, service design and sector-building work. Not every commission uses every stage, but the logic should remain visible.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 1. Start with people and place · What it means: Understand lived experience, local context, cultural history, relationships and existing knowledge.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 2. Frame the real question · What it means: Separate the stated brief from the underlying decision, need or tension.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 3. Map the system · What it means: Identify people, institutions, assets, incentives, gaps, power, dependencies and constraints.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 4. Build the evidence · What it means: Combine qualitative insight, public and commercial data, policy evidence, primary research and appropriate economic analysis.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 5. Make value visible · What it means: Show economic, cultural, social, civic, spatial and public-health value without reducing culture to one metric.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 6. Create shared meaning · What it means: Help different groups understand the evidence, the issue and each other.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 7. Design practical routes forward · What it means: Turn findings into choices, recommendations, asks, prototypes, governance, tools, investment cases and delivery plans.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 8. Leave useful infrastructure behind · What it means: Create evidence, skills, relationships, templates and systems that remain useful after the commission.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Do not treat participation as decoration.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Do not confuse data volume with evidence quality.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Do not claim neutrality where choices and values are involved.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Do not reduce cultural value to economic value, but do not ignore economic reality.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Make limitations, assumptions and disagreements visible.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Design recommendations around who can act, with what authority, resource and timeframe.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: Nightlife Culture should sound able to move between the dancefloor, the committee room, the funder meeting and the evidence base without losing the truth of the culture.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Joy → value → evidence → action.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Start with what people and places create. Explain what systems miss or obstruct. Build the evidence. End with a meaningful next step. Risk papers and funding cases may need to open with a problem, but they should restore people, value and agency quickly.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Human writing understands who is reading, gives enough context, acknowledges uncertainty, uses real examples and makes clear why something matters. It does not require forced slang, chatty filler, fake intimacy, constant rhetorical questions or emotional overstatement.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Culturally literate · Use it like this: Understand that scenes are built through trust, taste, memory, risk, work and timing. · Avoid: Explaining the sector to itself or performing authenticity.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Plainspoken · Use it like this: Make complex ideas understandable without flattening them. Use active verbs and clear asks. · Avoid: Consultancy sludge, inflated abstractions or unnecessary opacity.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Warm · Use it like this: Write to people, not at them. Respect time, knowledge and lived experience. · Avoid: Institutional distance, rescue language or fake intimacy.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Precise · Use it like this: Name evidence, uncertainty, exclusion and structural problems accurately. · Avoid: Vague critique, unsupported certainty or softened truth.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Generous · Use it like this: Recognise capability, value and knowledge before proposing something new. · Avoid: Defining people or places only through failure or need.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Constructive · Use it like this: Show what can happen next and who can act. · Avoid: Confusing critique with hopelessness or empty optimism.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: The voice should remain recognisably Nightlife Culture. Tone changes according to audience, purpose, risk and format.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Public and sector communications · Tone: Direct, warm, culturally literate · What to emphasise: People, place, lived reality, concrete meaning and action.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Policy and technical reports · Tone: Precise, structured, evidence-led · What to emphasise: Definitions, methods, assumptions, classifications and feasibility.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Decision briefings · Tone: Concise, calm, decision-ready · What to emphasise: The question, evidence, options, risks, recommendation and owner.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Funding and investment · Tone: Ambitious but grounded · What to emphasise: Need, value, method, outcomes, governance and delivery confidence.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Research and academic work · Tone: Transparent, rigorous, appropriately technical · What to emphasise: Sources, methods, limitations, reproducibility and interpretation.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Workshops and learning · Tone: Invitational, clear, paced · What to emphasise: Purpose, steps, examples, participation and usable takeaways.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Use these ideas where they are accurate, not as automatic slogans: collective joy; scenes; gathering places; cultural infrastructure; informal knowledge; trust, care and graft; conditions to thrive; people who make the night happen; shared asks; practical frameworks; sector knowledge; talent incubation; cultural value; evidence with soul.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Nightlife Culture does not avoid specialist, academic or policy language where it is the most accurate language for the job.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Terms such as regeneration, placemaking, resilience, creative industries, meanwhile use, stakeholder and ecosystem may have specific meanings within economic development, planning, research, funding and public policy. Use them where that meaning is relevant, particularly in technical reports, policy recommendations, planning documents, funding cases and work written for professional audiences.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: The aim is not to simplify complex ideas until they lose their meaning. We can write with intellectual and methodological rigour while remaining clear, human and rooted in the people and places that make nightlife happen.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Plain English is not anti-intellectual. It makes meaning available without removing complexity.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Technical and professional documents · Rule: Use the recognised term when precision, comparability or alignment with policy requires it.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Public communications · Rule: Translate specialist language into clear, concrete language without losing the meaning.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Vague or contested terms · Rule: Specify who or what the term refers to, what action is proposed and who benefits.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Precision versus informality · Rule: Do not replace a precise term simply to sound informal. Do not use a technical term to sound authoritative.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Vibrancy · Use it when: It is defined through specific activity, time, place or indicator. · Check for: Whether it is vague, exclusionary or visually coded.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Resilience · Use it when: It describes a system capacity, tested condition or defined risk. · Check for: Whether responsibility is being shifted onto under-resourced people.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Innovation · Use it when: Something is genuinely new or newly applied. · Check for: Whether practical improvement would be more accurate.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Inclusion · Use it when: The group, barrier, mechanism and outcome are named. · Check for: Whether the term hides unequal power or access.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Regeneration · Use it when: It has a planning, funding or policy meaning relevant to the work. · Check for: Who benefits, what may be displaced and whose place is being remade.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Activation · Use it when: It describes a specific intervention, use or programme. · Check for: Whether it implies a place was empty before institutional action.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Stakeholder · Use it when: It is useful in technical governance or project documentation. · Check for: Whether people, partners, residents, workers or sector voices would be more accurate.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Community · Use it when: A defined group, place or relationship is meant. · Check for: Whether differences in interest and power are being hidden.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Placemaking · Use it when: It is a recognised planning or practice term needed for the audience. · Check for: Whether it erases people already making and caring for the place.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Ecosystem · Use it when: Relationships and interdependencies are genuinely being analysed. · Check for: Whether it is replacing a more precise description.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: World-class · Use it when: There is a stated comparison and credible evidence. · Check for: Unsupported boosterism.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Meanwhile use · Use it when: It describes a specific temporary planning or property arrangement. · Check for: Whether cultural users are expected to absorb insecurity for others' benefit.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Creative industries · Use it when: The official sector definition or policy category is relevant. · Check for: Which subsectors and classifications are included or excluded.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Frontload the point.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Mix sentence lengths naturally.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Break long sentences where ideas compete.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Prefer concrete verbs to abstract nouns.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Use headings and short sections to guide the reader.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Use examples that are real and relevant.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Cut filler, repetition and AI-style platitudes.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Do not invent specificity, statistics or quotes.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Keep nuance where it changes meaning.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Avoid formulaic phrases such as “this matters”, “here is the bit everyone misses”, “in today’s rapidly changing landscape”, “unlock the potential”, “at the heart of”, “more important than ever” and repetitive three-part slogans unless the wording is genuinely earned by the content.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Nightlife and music communities · What they need: Recognition, respect, relevance and practical value. · Evidence emphasis: Lived experience, operating reality, rights, resources and exclusion.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Local and combined authorities · What they need: Clarity, legitimacy, feasibility and implementable choices. · Evidence emphasis: Policy, public data, statutory context, finance and delivery.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Funders and foundations · What they need: A credible need, method, outcomes and governance. · Evidence emphasis: Equity, impact, learning, evaluation and sustainability.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Cultural organisations and venues · What they need: Useful tools, shared leverage and realistic routes to action. · Evidence emphasis: Sector evidence, costs, capacity and precedents.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Researchers and universities · What they need: Methodological transparency and intellectual contribution. · Evidence emphasis: Sources, classifications, limitations, ethics and reproducibility.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Developers and place investors · What they need: Long-term value, stewardship, risk and opportunity. · Evidence emphasis: Place value, cultural infrastructure, footfall, displacement.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: National government and representative bodies · What they need: Scalable learning, policy relevance and clear asks. · Evidence emphasis: Comparative evidence, policy fit, implementation and accountability.
statements.subject: voice

statements.statement: Nightlife Culture’s credibility depends on how evidence is gathered, classified, interpreted and communicated. Strong design must never make weak evidence look stronger than it is.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Distinguish fact, estimate, interpretation, assumption and recommendation.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Cite the original source wherever possible.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: State publication date, data period, geography and population.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Explain sector definitions and classifications, including SIC codes where relevant.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Identify proprietary, commercial and restricted data.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Describe primary research methods, recruitment, sample size and limitations.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Do not imply causation from correlation.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Avoid unsupported economic-impact multipliers and false precision.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Separate commissioned evidence from independent evidence.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Record uncertainty, missing data, disagreement and methodological judgement.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Link recommendations to evidence and identify who can act.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Every data visual, table or significant factual claim should enable the reader to trace the evidence. Link to the specific dataset, publication or page rather than an organisation homepage where possible.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: What is being recommended? · Required answer: A specific action, choice or principle.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Why? · Required answer: The evidence and reasoning.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Who can act? · Required answer: Named institution, role, partnership or sector.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: What is required? · Required answer: Authority, funding, capacity, data, policy change or collaboration.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: When? · Required answer: Timeframe or decision point.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: How will we know? · Required answer: Outcome, indicator, review or learning mechanism.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: What could go wrong? · Required answer: Risk, trade-off, unintended effect or dependency.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: This section is the communications-facing summary. The full standard — provenance codes, minimum source metadata, the indicator comparability gate, classification versioning, ethics and the recommendation strength scale — lives in Comparative Place-Based Research Methodology v1.0. Where the two documents touch, the methodology governs. Section 12 of this guide translates its requirements into chart and layout components.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Every accent is a black-text surface. Every ground is a white-text surface. There are no exceptions and no judgement calls. White on pink is 2.62:1 and fails; white on violet is 2.54:1 and fails; black on blue is 2.44:1 and fails. If you remember one thing from this section, remember this sentence.

statements.statement: Because the five accents share a lightness register, every pair sits between 1.01 and 1.98:1. They are distinguished by hue alone. In greyscale, on a projector, or for a reader with a colour vision deficiency they collapse into one another.

statements.statement: Roles, not adjacency, keep them apart. Pink is the small hot mark, teal the cool highlight, violet the calm surface, butter the warm one, coral the urgent one. Give each a job and they never need to be told apart at a glance.

statements.statement: Colour is never the only carrier of meaning. Test every foreground and background combination. Use WCAG thresholds: at least 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text, and 3:1 for meaningful graphics and interface components.

statements.statement: Do not reduce opacity on essential text.

statements.statement: Note on the 3:1 graphics threshold. It applies to graphics required to understand content and to interface components. A coloured panel that is simply a surface holding high-contrast text is neither — the text carries the contrast. Panel outlines are a style choice, not an accessibility requirement. The threshold does apply to chart series, meaningful icons and strokes, focus states, and any edge that itself carries meaning.

statements.statement: H1 · Face: Archivo ExtraBold 800 · Case: ALL CAPS · Rule: Tracking +1%. Eight words maximum — break to two lines rather than shrinking.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: H2 · Face: Archivo ExtraBold 800 · Case: ALL CAPS · Rule: Tracking +4%. Caps tighten optically as they shrink; the tracking compensates.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: H3 · Face: Archivo Bold 700 · Case: Sentence case · Rule: The floor. Caps stop working below roughly 16pt on screen and in long reports.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Body · Face: Inter Regular 400 · Case: Sentence case · Rule: Never caps. Line height 1.5–1.6 for running prose — see the scoped table below. Left-aligned, never justified.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Labels / meta · Face: Archivo SemiBold 600 · Case: ALL CAPS · Rule: Tracking +8–16%. Short strings only — three or four words.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: All-caps headings are core to how Nightlife Culture looks. They also carry a readability cost, which falls hardest on dyslexic and low-vision readers. The rule is caps with guardrails, not caps with an exception:
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Always tracked. Every caps level above carries a letter-spacing value. That is the mitigation, not a styling preference — untracked caps are measurably harder to read.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Never below 16pt on screen or 14pt in print. Below that, caps lose the word-shape cues that make scanning possible.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Eight words maximum, two lines maximum. Caps are for statements, not sentences.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: H3 and below stay sentence case. In a long report, all-caps sub-headings are tiring and the brand gains least at that level.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Never caps in body copy, captions, source lines, alt text or table cells.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Screen readers handle capitalised words correctly when the caps are applied as formatting. Caps are never typed: use text-transform: uppercase in HTML and the All Caps character format in Word and PowerPoint. Typed capitals destroy the underlying string for search, copy-paste, translation and some assistive-technology configurations — and the damage is invisible in the rendered result, so it survives every visual review. Tracked, short and above 16pt, caps are defensible. Untracked and long, they are not.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Left-align body text. Do not justify.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Use bold more often than italics for emphasis.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Reserve underlining primarily for links.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Use 12pt body text in documents where practical, with 1.5 to 1.6 line spacing in running prose. Other style classes set their own — see below.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Remove copy before reducing type.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Slide titles · Minimum: 32pt · Preferred: 38–52pt
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Slide body · Minimum: 18pt · Preferred: 20–26pt
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Slide labels · Minimum: 14pt · Preferred: 16pt+
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Document body · Minimum: 12pt · Preferred: 12pt
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Footnotes and caveats · Minimum: 10pt · Preferred: 10.5–11pt. A caveat that matters belongs in the title, column heading or row label, not a footnote. A caveat that does not matter should be deleted.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: WCAG SC 1.4.8 sets 1.5 as the floor for line spacing within paragraphs. It was never a rule about table cells, slide bullets, captions or headings. Applied as a blanket it produces two specific failures: display type at 1.5 reads limp, and a table at 1.5 stops scanning across, because rows are read horizontally and generous leading pulls them apart.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Display, H1 · Document: 1.02–1.1 · HTML: 1.02–1.1 · Slide: 1.02–1.1 · Why: Tight leading is what makes display type read as a unit.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: H2, H3 · Document: 1.15–1.25 · HTML: 1.2–1.3 · Slide: 1.15–1.25 · Why: Short lines; leading is spacing, not readability.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Running prose · Document: 1.5–1.6 · HTML: 1.5–1.6 · Slide: 1.25–1.4 · Why: The only place SC 1.4.8 applies. Slides rarely carry paragraphs.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Slide body, bullets · Document: — · HTML: — · Slide: 1.2–1.35 · Why: Few lines, short measure, read at distance.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Table cells · Document: 1.25–1.35 · HTML: 1.25–1.35 · Slide: 1.2–1.3 · Why: Not paragraphs. Tight is more readable — rows must stay scannable.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Captions, source lines · Document: 1.3–1.4 · HTML: 1.3–1.4 · Slide: 1.25–1.35 · Why: Short, secondary, one or two lines.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Statistic blocks · Document: 1.0–1.1 · HTML: 1.0–1.1 · Slide: 1.0–1.1 · Why: A number is not text.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Lists · Document: 1.4–1.5 · HTML: 1.4–1.5 · Slide: 1.25–1.35 · Why: Space between items does the work.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Only the running-prose row is Fixed. Everything else is Adaptable — the rule is that the value is scoped, not that these particular numbers are correct. The same scoping applies to measure, minimum size and alignment.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Archivo Black, Archivo and Inter are open-licence (SIL Open Font License). Embed them in every digital deliverable — never link them from a web font service. A linked font fails silently and falls back to a system sans, which is how a deck can look wrong on someone else's machine without anyone noticing. Where a font cannot be embedded, the approved fallback stack is Arial, then the system sans.
statements.subject: type

statements.statement: Contain with colour and space, not with outlines.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Panels are held by fill, rule or space. Hard black outlines are retired — they were doing the work that space should do, and they made every panel shout at the same volume.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Fill. The colour field is the container. The default for accent panels. Needs space around it.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Top rule. White panel, 9px accent bar. Dense pages, tables and long documents.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Left rule. Reads as an aside rather than a box. Pull quotes and callouts.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Band. Runs edge to edge. Stops being a panel and becomes a change of ground.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Hairline. 1px ink at 22%. White boxes on chalk, tables, dense reference layouts.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Fill · Spec: Accent background, no border · Use: Default for accent panels. Requires generous surrounding space.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Top rule · Spec: White panel, 9px accent bar · Use: Dense pages, tables, long documents where five filled panels would be too much.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Left rule · Spec: White panel, 12px accent bar · Use: Pull quotes, callouts, asides.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Full-bleed band · Spec: Accent or ink, edge to edge · Use: Slides and covers. How an accent leads without looking like a box.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Hairline · Spec: 1px ink at 22% · Use: White panels on a chalk ground, tables, forms. Never for anything carrying meaning.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: Hard outline · Spec: — · Use: Retired.
statements.subject: containment

statements.statement: One main idea per slide or section where possible.
statements.subject: layout

statements.statement: Use space as part of the voice.
statements.subject: layout

statements.statement: Use blue as a structural signal rather than scattered decoration.
statements.subject: layout

statements.statement: Avoid dense boxes, tiny labels and decorative clutter.
statements.subject: layout

statements.statement: Keep core information in a simple reading order.
statements.subject: layout

statements.statement: Use single-column layouts for long-form accessible documents where practical.
statements.subject: layout

statements.statement: Chalk ground, white panels. Or white ground, panels held by a rule.
statements.subject: layout

statements.statement: Side margins · Measure: 6% of slide width · Rule: Nothing crosses them.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Top margin · Measure: 7.5% of slide height · Rule: Kicker sits on this line.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Footer band · Measure: Bottom 14% · Rule: Content never enters it. Logo and slide number only.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Body measure · Measure: Max 60–70% of content width · Rule: The ragged right edge is part of the composition.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Title zone · Measure: Three lines maximum · Rule: Four lines means the statement is a paragraph.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Coverage · Measure: Roughly half the canvas empty · Rule: More than about 55% covered means it is two slides.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: “Remove copy before reducing type” is the rule that protects all the others.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Blue — primary · Section header: Teal · Use: Section dividers, statements, two-column contrast, quotes. Top rules, nothing boxed. The workhorse.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Chalk / white · Section header: Blue · Use: Working ground. Charcoal title, blue sub. Colour blocks or a vertical third. Chalk in decks, white in reports.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Ink · Section header: Teal · Use: Night register, used sparingly. Accent blocks, or a full-bleed strip under a light slide.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Accents · Section header: — · Use: Blocks, thirds, strips and cells. Never a full-bleed accent ground.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Which ground, for which room. Light ground is the default whenever the venue is unconfirmed. Ambient light lifts a projector's blacks asymmetrically, so an ink deck greys out in a lit room at 11am — and blue on ink is 2.26:1 by our own matrix. Ink requires a darkened room, confirmed in advance, and every ink deck ships with a light-ground variant.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Blue — primary. Teal kicker, teal separator, no logo on a content slide.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Chalk — working ground. Charcoal title, blue sub, blue separator.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: A breaker is a pause, not an ornament. One per slide. Two rules and it stops meaning “pause” and starts meaning “pattern”.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Separator · Weight and width: 0.42% of slide width · 20% wide · Colour: Blue on light, teal on dark · Where: Between the title zone and the body zone, flush to the left margin. The default.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Hairline · Weight and width: 1px · 74% wide · Colour: Ink at 22% · Where: Under the title on dense or document-register slides.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Stop · Weight and width: 0.42% · 20% wide · Colour: Teal · Where: Under a divider title, with nothing following it.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Accent bar · Weight and width: 0.55% · 14–22% wide · Colour: Pink · Where: Above a pull quote. The only decorative use, and always at the top.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Retired: a rule breaking the middle of a statement. It interrupts the sentence rather than pacing it.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Two-digit, bottom-right, Archivo ExtraBold at 1.25% of slide width. Charcoal on light grounds, teal on dark. Content slides only — not the cover, not the closing slide. Numbered by position in the deck, not by section.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: They matter because people cite slides in meetings, funders and officers reference them in writing, decks get printed and reordered, and position in a sequence is orientation that should not exist only in a scrollbar.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: The wordmark is an outlined asset. It is never re-set as live type.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: That sentence is the whole rule. Everything below explains why, so nobody is tempted to fudge it.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: nightlife-culture-wordmark.svg · Use: Inline in HTML. Inherits currentColor — set color on the parent.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: nightlife-culture-wordmark-white.svg · Use: On blue, ink, or any dark ground. For .
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: nightlife-culture-wordmark-blue.svg · Use: On chalk or white. For .
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: nightlife-culture-wordmark-ink.svg · Use: On an accent ground. For .
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: All four are outlined vector paths. They render identically whether or not Archivo Black is installed. currentColor does not work through — use a coloured variant there.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: The wordmark comes from the printed business card. Measured from that artwork:
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: NIGHTLIFE · Value: 32.09pt
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: CULTURE · Value: 33.41pt
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Rendered width, NIGHTLIFE · Value: 171.92pt
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Rendered width, CULTURE · Value: 171.19pt
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Baseline to baseline · Value: 30.41pt
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Effective line-height · Value: 0.9476
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: The two lines are set at different sizes so they justify to the same width — 171.92 against 171.19, a difference of 0.4%. That is what makes the lockup read as a solid rectangle rather than a ragged stack.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Set both lines at one size and you lose it. Every regenerated version has made exactly that mistake, including the nightlife-culture-lockup.svg in the design-system development folder, which is live <text> at a single size with letter-spacing:-3 — a rendering of type, not the mark.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Never re-set as live type. Not in HTML, not in PowerPoint, not in Figma, not in a prompt. Place the SVG.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Never restack, re-space or re-track it. The relationship between the two lines is the mark.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Never stretch it. Scale proportionally. No preserveAspectRatio="none", no dragging a corner without a modifier key.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: One colour only. White on blue and ink. Blue on chalk and white. Ink on an accent. The two-colour treatment (charcoal + one accent) is permitted on covers only.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Teal is never a logo colour on a light ground — 1.52:1 on white. Pink (7.42:1) and violet (7.64:1) are the accents that clear it.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Clear space: at least the cap height of NIGHTLIFE on all four sides. Nothing enters it.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Minimum size: 90px wide on screen, 22mm in print. Below that, use the wordmark on one line or omit it.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Never place it on photography without a tested solid surface behind it.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Never add anything to it — no strapline locked up, no box, no rule, no shadow, no outline.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Never two logos on one surface.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Each swatch below is a ground, not a specimen. No wordmark is drawn on this page, because drawing one here would mean re-setting it as type — the exact thing rule 1 forbids. The slot shows where the placed SVG goes and which file to use.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Chalk or white ground. Blue wordmark. The footer default.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Blue ground. White wordmark. Never teal — teal is the section header.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Ink ground. White wordmark.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Accent ground. Ink wordmark. Two-colour (charcoal + one accent) is permitted on covers only, never in a footer.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Slides — cover, dividers, closing · Rule: Full lockup.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Slides — content · Rule: No logo by default. The exception is any slide likely to travel alone — a headline finding, a data slide, a quote. If you would screenshot it, mark it.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Slide footer version · Rule: Approximately 1.5% of slide width. It should be the quietest thing there.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Documents · Rule: Cover and back page only. Never in a running header.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: Everything else · Rule: Once. Quietly.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: If you need something this section does not cover: say so and stop. Do not improvise a variant. A logo that gets improvised is not a logo.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: The masthead and footer now carry the placed outlined wordmark, inline, inheriting currentColor. Earlier versions set them as live Archivo Black at a single size — the exact failure described above, in the guide's own furniture.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: The four SVGs were regenerated from the measurements in this section and verified against them: NIGHTLIFE renders at 171.92pt, CULTURE at 171.19pt, the two lines justifying to within 0.42%. Tracking differs per line by design (−0.0872em and −0.0264em) — that is what makes two different sizes finish at the same width.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: If a regenerated mark does not reproduce those two widths, it is not the mark. Do not ship it.
statements.subject: logo

statements.statement: The brand accents cannot carry data. This ramp can — the same hues, stepped in lightness so the series stay distinct in greyscale, on a projector and for a colourblind reader.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: The grey strip is the same four series desaturated. Lightness climbs monotonically (0.45 → 0.58 → 0.75 → 0.91), so the order survives photocopying, greyscale printing, projection, deuteranopia and tritanopia. Under protanopia the order inverts: series 1 and 2 converge to 1.10:1, effectively one colour. Wherever both appear in the same chart, differentiate them by more than colour — a dashed stroke, a marker, or a direct label. The label-at-the-mark rule already covers most cases. The brand accents do not have this property and cannot, if they are to stay harmonious.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Series 1 · Hex: #0000FF · OKLCH L: 0.45 · Labels: White
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Series 2 · Hex: #C7339A · OKLCH L: 0.58 · Labels: White
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Series 3 · Hex: #00C6C5 · OKLCH L: 0.75 · Labels: Ink
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Series 4 · Hex: #FFDE6B · OKLCH L: 0.91 · Labels: Ink
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Four series maximum · Why: Beyond four the ramp stops being distinguishable. Five categories means a bar chart with direct labels, not more colours.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: One series = blue · Why: The ramp is for genuinely different series. A single-series chart in four colours implies a distinction that is not there.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Label at the mark · Why: Values on bars, series names at the end of lines, percentages in the key. Legends are a last resort.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Never brand accents · Why: Pink, teal, violet, butter and coral are surfaces. Only the ramp encodes data.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Show the gaps · Why: Hatched fill for suppressed, dashed line for a break in collection. Never a silent omission — a gap in the data is a finding.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Show the range · Why: Modelled or surveyed values get a visible interval. A bare point estimate reads as a count.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Provenance on every chart · Why: Code, reference period, geography and boundary vintage.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Flag illustrative figures · Why: Any placeholder or worked example says so, in the chart, every time.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Gridlines at 10% ink · Why: Present enough to read against, quiet enough to disappear. Never heavier than the data.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Alt text describes the finding · Why: Not “line chart of venue counts” but what the chart shows. Plus a data table alternative for anything load-bearing.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: No non-uniform scaling · Why: An SVG or image never gets stretched to fit. The container flexes; the coordinate space does not. Stretching destroys the type.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Separator on segmented forms · Why: Donuts and 100% stacked bars have segments that touch. Adjacent ramp contrast in greyscale is 1.79, 2.27 and 1.61 — all below the 3:1 threshold for meaningful graphics. A 1–2px white or ink hairline between adjacent segments closes it. The ramp is rated for separated, labelled marks; not for shared edges.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Ranked horizontal bar · When: The workhorse. Categories with a magnitude. Ranked descending unless the categories have a natural order.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Dot plot · When: Comparing places. Bars imply a quantity from zero; dots imply a position on a scale, which is what an indicator is — and leave room for the plausible range.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: 100% stacked bar · When: Comparing two or more wholes. Replaces most pies.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Donut · When: One whole, four segments maximum, percentages always in the key. The hole carries the total.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Pie · When: Permitted, with the caveat that angles are read less accurately than lengths. Justified when one dominant share needs to be instantly recognisable. Same four-segment limit.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Line · When: Change over time. Series labelled at the line, never in a legend. Dashed segments for breaks in collection — never interpolate across one.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Range bar · When: Anywhere uncertainty is material.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: [c] suppressed for disclosure control. The row stays; the gap is visible. ADM-OPEN 2025 · LA boundary 2023 · illustrative figures.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: These components come from Comparative Place-Based Research Methodology v1.0. They are not decorative.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Three tiers: ink for open and traceable, butter for documented-but-partial, coral for opaque or untraceable. The code text carries the meaning on its own, so the tier survives greyscale and screen readers. Coral does not mean “bad” — it means “handle with a stated caveat”.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: OFF-OPEN · ADM-OPEN · ADM-RESTRICTED · ACADEMIC · PRI-OPEN
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: SECTOR · COM-DOCUMENTED · PRI-DOCUMENTED
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: COM-PARTIAL · COM-BLACKBOX · PRI-OPAQUE · ANECDOTAL · UNTRACEABLE
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Any chart comparing two or more places states whether the indicator comparability gate has been cleared, and which of the eight criteria required harmonisation. A comparison without this note is not publishable.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: The 1–5 scale shown as filled ordinal steps in ink, never as a colour scale — strength is ordinal, so it is shown by how much is filled. Readable in greyscale, and it cannot be mistaken for a red/amber/green judgement. The level is always written out alongside.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Every big number carries a source line by default: reference period, geography, boundary vintage and provenance code. A statistic without them is a claim, not a finding, and the evidence standard separates the two.
statements.subject: data

statements.statement: Accessibility is a design standard, not finishing polish.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: When brand and accessibility conflict, accessibility wins. Move the brand to layout, rhythm, typography, covers, pattern, photography or non-essential decoration rather than weakening the meaning layer.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Fixed · Examples: Semantic headings, readable size, contrast, links, reading order, focus states, alt text · Rule: Do not override for brand preference.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Adaptable · Examples: Logo scale, exact colour tint, spacing, page composition, chart styling · Rule: Adjust to user, format and accessibility needs.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Decorative · Examples: Patterns, textures, overlays, flourishes, non-informational imagery · Rule: May be removed without losing meaning.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Meet WCAG 2.2 AA as the minimum standard; aim higher where practical.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Choose the format from the user need, not production habit.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Publish HTML first for public information where practical.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Use real headings, lists and table structures.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Use descriptive links, never “click here”.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Add useful alt text to meaningful images and mark decorative images appropriately.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Do not use images of text when live text will work.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Provide text or data alternatives for charts and diagrams.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Check reading order before PDF publication.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Set document title and language metadata.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: Test with automated checks and manual review.
statements.subject: accessibility

statements.statement: [c] already marks a suppressed value. This is the rule that decides when to use it.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: No published figure rests on fewer than three contributing units.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Where a cell falls below the threshold, suppress it and apply secondary suppression, so the value cannot be recovered by subtraction from row or column totals.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Keep category structures fixed across editions. Two differently-cut tables of the same population can be differenced against each other to recover what neither shows.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: If more than half a table is suppressed, change the geography or the categories rather than publishing holes.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Statistic blocks carry a minimum base. A big number is the most-screenshotted thing we produce; one derived from four people travels further than the caveat does.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: State the disclosure treatment in the provenance chip.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Decide disclosure-safe granularity before designing to a granularity, not after.
statements.subject: evidence

statements.statement: Use Heading 1, Heading 2 and Heading 3 styles in a logical hierarchy.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Set the document title, author or organisation, and language in properties.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Use built-in list styles.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Use table headers and repeat header rows across pages.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Do not use spaces, tabs or blank paragraphs for layout.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Use page breaks rather than repeated returns.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Avoid essential information in headers or footers only.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Run the Microsoft Accessibility Checker and manually check complex layouts.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: White ground, not chalk — Word and print handle white more predictably, and partners will edit it.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Every slide carries a unique, descriptive title. It may be positioned off-canvas or hidden. It may not be absent — it is how screen-reader users navigate a deck, and the title list doubles as the deck's outline.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Set reading order explicitly in the Selection Pane, on every slide. Reading order follows shape-creation order and bears no relation to visual position. Decorative shapes marked decorative, and last.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Build on restyled master layouts, never manually placed text boxes. Built-in layouts keep reading order aligned with visual order.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: No text box sized to its text. A substituted face widens the same string by roughly a third. Font embedding prevents most substitution; this is the second line of defence.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: No tables on slides. A table on a slide is a reference table in the wrong artefact — put it in the leave-behind.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Run the Accessibility Checker before export. Decks leave as tagged PDF; the .pptx goes only to people who must edit it.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: Export from a structured source; do not print to PDF.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Verify tags, headings, reading order, links, alt text, title and language.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Use bookmarks in longer reports.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Ensure text is selectable and searchable.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Check zoom, reflow and page order.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Provide another accessible format where a fixed-layout PDF is not enough.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: The conclusion sits in the first screen, in every format.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: Headings state findings, not topics. “Referrals fell 34%” not “Referral trends”. A contents list built from finding-headings is a readable summary, which is what most readers use it as.
statements.subject: documents

statements.statement: No skipped heading levels. H2 to H4 breaks outline navigation.

statements.statement: Real bookmarks in every PDF, generated from heading styles — not a typeset contents page.

statements.statement: Before designing, establish whether the structure is mandated, expected or free. Where a funder or commissioner names a model — a Five Case business case, an evaluation framework, their own form or response schedule — follow it exactly. Brand expression lives inside the required structure, never in place of it. A bid can be on-brand, accessible and beautifully set, and still be marked down for answering in the wrong shape.

statements.statement: 1 · The dense layout tier. Everything specified in section 10 is the generous register — one idea, half the canvas empty. Content-heavy slides need a second tier with its own margins, type sizes and coverage ceiling. Without it the system will be broken the first time a slide carries five or six blocks, and then there is no rule at all. Until v1.1: hold the 6% margins and the 14% footer band, allow coverage up to 70%, drop slide body to the 18pt minimum, and cap at six blocks.
statements.subject: slides

statements.statement: 2 · Diagram components. No diagram system exists yet. PowerPoint SmartArt will fight every rule in this guide — it picks its own colours, type, spacing and outlines. v1.1 will provide a diagram kit (nodes, connectors, numbering, stage labels, axis) rather than fixed templates, so new patterns can be built without leaving the system. Until then: build diagrams from the containment treatments in section 09 and the chart ramp in section 12, and do not use SmartArt defaults.
statements.subject: layout

statements.subject: layout

statements.statement: 3 · Templates. Deck master, Word template and an HTML component sheet follow this guide rather than accompanying it — otherwise the templates become the spec and the guide becomes decoration.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 4 · Dashboards. No dashboard system exists yet, and one should not be built casually. Until it does: a dashboard is only justified where research shows users need to explore, where the data updates automatically, where users genuinely need different cuts, and where there is funding to maintain it beyond launch. All four. Otherwise the answer is a release, a report, or an accessible spreadsheet. If one is built, the default view must answer the main question before any filter is touched, the whole thing must work from the keyboard including the charts, and disclosure thresholds must be enforced at query time on every filter combination — not just the default view.

statements.statement: 0.1 · Date: July 2026 · Main changes: Initial working guide for brand, voice, visual identity, accessibility and production.

statements.statement: 0.2 · Date: July 2026 · Main changes: Expanded voice and human-writing guidance; added accessible production standards.

statements.statement: 0.3 · Date: July 2026 · Main changes: Broadened positioning and territory; defined the Nightlife Culture method.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 1.0 · Date: August 2026 · Main changes: Full replacement of the visual and production system. New eight-token palette tuned in OKLCH, replacing the four-colour palette. Chalk and white grounds replacing cream. Archivo Black / Archivo ExtraBold / Inter replacing Aptos and Arial. All-caps heading rule with tracking guardrails, replacing sentence-case headings. Containment system replacing hard outlines. Breaker system, slide grid, logo rules and slide numbering added. Four-series chart ramp and evidence furniture added, aligned to the research methodology. Brand foundation, method, voice, language, audience and evidence sections carried forward from v0.3 with light editing. Known gaps recorded in section 15.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 1.4 · Date: August 2026 · Main changes: The wordmark is now placed, not typeset. Masthead and footer carry the outlined SVG inline. The four variants were regenerated from the section 11 measurements and verified against them — NIGHTLIFE 171.92pt, CULTURE 171.19pt, justifying to 0.42%. Tracking differs per line (−0.0872em / −0.0264em), which is what lets two sizes finish at one width.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 1.3 · Date: August 2026 · Main changes: Logo section replaced in full. The wordmark is an outlined asset and is never re-set as live type — the previous section described it as “Archivo Black, tight leading” and rendered four live-type specimens, which is the failure the rule exists to prevent. Adds the four SVG variants, the measurements from the printed card (NIGHTLIFE 32.09pt, CULTURE 33.41pt, set at different sizes so both lines justify to the same width), ten rules, minimum size, clear space, and the instruction to stop rather than improvise a variant. Ground swatches now show which file to place, and deliberately draw no wordmark.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 1.2 · Date: August 2026 · Main changes: Line height scoped by style class and context. 1.5–1.6 was resolved in v1.1 as a single value; that is the running-prose value and was never a rule for table cells, captions, display or statistics. A scoped table now sets each. Table cells 1.25–1.35 — tight is more readable, because rows are read across. Only running prose is Fixed.
statements.subject: process

statements.statement: 1.1 · Date: August 2026 · Main changes: Eleven amendments following a full review against The Decision Book. Protanopia exception added to the chart ramp (measured: series 1 and 2 converge to 1.10:1). Line height resolved to a single 1.5–1.6 floor, stated once. Document body minimum raised to 12pt. Caps mechanism specified as formatting, never typed. Separator required on segmented charts. Disclosure control added. PowerPoint, long-form and mandated-structure sections added. Room rule added for slide grounds. Dashboard gate added to Known gaps.
statements.subject: process
